dialogue.title: First meeting
lines: My name is Brune. And you?
My name is Xiao Li. What country are you from?

shi.title: 是 (shì) — the verb "to be"
shi.body: 是 (shì) is like the verb "to be," but with an important difference: it only links nouns to each other, never a noun to an adjective. And Chinese verbs are never conjugated — the form of 是 doesn't change in the present, past or future.

shi.title: "Wǒ shì Měiguó rén" or "wǒ jiào Brune"?
shi.body: Shì links you to a category — nationality, profession, identity. Jiào (叫) is used only to say your name. Notice that "my name is" never uses shì in Chinese — only jiào.

svo-order.title: Basic sentence order: Subject + Verb + Object
svo-order.body: The most common sentence structure in Chinese follows the same order as English: subject, then verb, then object. Changing the position of the words changes the meaning of the sentence.

shi-drop-casual.title: "Wǒ shì Měiguó rén" sometimes drops the "shì"
shi-drop-casual.body: In fast, very casual speech, you may hear 我美国人 (wǒ Měiguó rén) without the 是 — the meaning is still clear from context. This is very informal and only works in short sentences like this. In the exercises here, keep writing the standard form with 是, which always sounds correct.

ordem-nomes-sobrenome-primeiro.title: In Chinese, the family name comes first
ordem-nomes-sobrenome-primeiro.body: Notice "小李" (Xiǎo Lǐ) in the dialogue: Lǐ is the family name, and it comes BEFORE the given name — the opposite of the usual English order. 小 (xiǎo, "small") is an affectionate, informal prefix, common among coworkers and close friends, used with the family name of someone younger or the same age.
examples: (affectionate nickname) "Li" — family name Lǐ + prefix 小

trueFalse.claim: This question is used to find out someone's nationality.
trueFalse.whyNote: Wrong — 你叫什么名字？ asks for the NAME (叫 = to be called, 名字 = name), not the nationality. Nationality would be "你是哪国人？".
